Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Ponderas Academic Hospital, part of the network of private healthcare provider Regina Maria, has opened a hybrid operating suite for the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular diseases following a EUR 1.7 million investment. The suite “enables interventional radiology procedures and image-guided, minimally invasive treatments, strengthening the hospital's capacity to manage complex cardiovascular surgery and interventional cardiology cases simultaneously,” it said. "The hybrid suite changes the options available to us when treating complex cardiovascular cases. Its main advantage is that it allows us to do more for patients in a less invasive way. Procedures that previously had to be performed in separate stages, requiring two hospital admissions and two rounds of anesthesia, can now be carried out during a single intervention. For patients, this means less time in hospital and an easier recovery," Dr. Cătălin Trifan, attending cardiovascular surgeon at Ponderas Academic Hospital, said. The hospital has nearly 400 inpatient beds, 38 day-care beds, 43 intensive care beds and 14 operating theatres. It also has three dedicated emergency departments: for adults, pediatrics, and obstetrics and gynecology. The hospital was established in 2010 as a center dedicated to bariatric and metabolic surgery. After its integration into the Regina Maria network in 2016, it expanded the range of medical specialties. Over the past few years, investments have exceeded EUR 20 million, helping to double the hospital's capacity while supporting annual growth in activity of more than 10%. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/25/vegr.text: Menü Kereső Varga Juditot és Rogán Antalt is meghallgatná a végrehajtási visszaéléseket vizsgáló bizottság Belföld frissítve Gulyás Ádám Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Közzétették a parlament honlapján , hogy kiket kötelezne nyilatkozattételre az Országgyűlés Végrehajtási Visszaéléseket Feltáró Vizsgálóbizottsága. A dokumentum szerint, a vizsgálóbizottság 65 személytől kérne nyilatkozatot írásbeli vagy szóbeli formában. A bizottság 5 témában hallgatna meg embereket, az egyik ilyen téma a Schadl-ügy lenne, amellyel kapcsolatban szóbeli nyilatkozattételre köteleznék: Schadl Györgyöt, a Magyar Bírósági Végrehajtói Kar volt elnökét, Völner Pál korábbi igazságügyi államtitkárt, Rogán Antalt, az Orbán-kormány Miniszterelnöki Kabinetirodájának vezetőjét, Nagy Ádámot, Rogán egykori kabinetfőnökét, valamint Rehák Róbert vállalkozót, a Schadl-ügy vádlottját. Írásban kell majd nyilatkozatot tennie Rogán Antal feleségének, Rogán Barbarának, illetve Schadl György feleségének, Schadl-Baranyai Helgának. A felügyeleti szervek, így az Igazságügyi Minisztérium és a Szabályozott Tevékenységek Felügyeleti Hatósága működésével kapcsolatban az Orbán-kormányok több igazságügyi miniszterét és államtitkárát is meghallgatnák: Draskovics Tibor korábbi igazságügyi és rendészeti minisztert, Navracsics Tibor volt közigazgatási és igazságügyi minisztert, Répássy Róbert egykori államtitkárt, Jeney Orsolya és Czepek Gábor volt helyettes államtitkárokat, továbbá Trócsányi László, Varga Judit és Tuzson Bence volt igazságügyi minisztereket. Ugyanebben a témában Dávid Ibolya volt igazságügyi minisztertől írásbeli beszámolót vár a bizottság. A parlament honlapjára felkerült dokumentum szerint Czine Ágnes alkotmánybírót is írásbeli nyilatkozattételre kötelezné a bizottság, ugyanakkor a bizottsági ülés közvetítésében az hangzik el, hogy habár egy korábbi listán Czine is szerepelt, végül mégsem hallgatja meg a bizottság. Az ellentmondással kapcsolatban megkerestük a bizottságot. A bizottság által nyilatkozattételre kötelezett személyeknek kötelező lesz megjelenniük, és igazat mondaniuk, a bizottságok jogköreit ugyanis júniusban komolyan szigorította az Országgyűlés . A Végrehajtási Visszaéléseket Feltáró Vizsgálóbizottság egyike annak az öt parlamenti vizsgálóbizottságnak, amelyek a Tisza Párt kezdeményezésére jöttek létre még júniusban, az elnöke a Mi Hazánk parlamenti frakcióját és magát a pártot is vezető Toroczkai László. Toroczkai már korábban jelezte, hogy 1994-től vizsgálná a felelősség kérdését, és egyebek mellett Orbán Viktort, Gyurcsány Ferencet, Rogán Antalt, korábbi minisztereket és képviselőket is meghallgatna. Előbbiek egyelőre azonban nem kerültek fel a most közzétett listára. Frissítés: cikkük korábbi verziójában az szerepelt, hogy Czine Ágnest írásbeli nyilatkozattételre kötelezné a bizottság, a bizottsági ülésről készült felvételen azonban az hangzik el, hogy Czine Ágnest mégse hallgatja meg a bizottság. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pw.text: Image source, Tennesse Department of Corrections Image caption, Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date By Stephanie Hegarty BBC World Service Correspondent Published 27 September 2026, 00:04 BST Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee. Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says. Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago. Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest. Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull. A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men. Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting". Image source, Family handout Image caption, Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped. , external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence. In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider. "It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence. "Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness." Image source, Christa Pike Image caption, Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parents In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened. But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge. In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since. Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her. "Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says. Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation." Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable." Image source, Christa Pike Image caption, Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say 'She should pay for it' Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution. A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy. Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021 . Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before. The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps. On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it. Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution. "She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments. Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did." Image source, J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via Reuters Image caption, May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006 "My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added. "There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting." The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution. The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want. "We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed." Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption. "When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says. "These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else." Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime. "People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says. "Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live." REUTERS/Tom Brenner/File Photo Raw Exclusive Trump loses 'biggest prize' as far-right leaders topple around the world: expert By: Kathleen Culliton Oct 27, 2026 8:00AM ET Kathleen Culliton Kathleen Culliton is a Raw Story investigations writer. She's been covering local and national news for more than a decade for outlets that include the New York Post, Al Jazeera, DNAinfo New York, Bustle, the New York Daily News, WNYC, NY1, City Limits and the New York City Patch. Kathleen is a proud alumna of the CUNY Graduate School of Journalism. SEE FULL BIO Make us preferred on Google Comments 0 Share Article A stunning electoral upset just lost President Donald Trump the "biggest prize" — as his allies abroad topple, a political expert told Raw Story on Monday. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's runoff victory Sunday against Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right son of a former president imprisoned for staging a coup, delivered a stinging blow to Trump's plans, Berea College Professor Carlos G. Poggio told Raw Story. "Lula’s victory represents a significant defeat for Donald Trump and [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio ," Poggio, a Brazilian political scientist, said in an email. "Brazil was the biggest prize in the conservative tide sweeping Latin America." The defeats for Trump are numerous and multifaceted — they span from the U.S. to Latin America and China and hit his power, and his wallet, Poggio argued. Bolsonaro, 45, had aligned himself with Trump by pledging to mine the Amazon rainforest for critical mineral deposits, which would ease U.S. dependence on Chinese rare earth exports , limited in 2025 in response to Trump's tariffs. Trump would also have had the support of Latin America's largest economy with a GDP of $2.65 trillion , according to data collected by independent statisticians at Worldometer, and the power such money can access. "A Flávio Bolsonaro government would likely have become Trump’s most important regional ally, supporting the Trump administration’s security agenda and closer U.S. access to Brazil’s critical minerals," Poggio said. That may be why the Bolsonaro family have had help from two officials from within Trump's State department since 2025, as a Reuters report revealed earlier this month. The officials, Darren Beattie and Ricardo Pita, first tried to reinstate former President Jair Bolsonaro, ousted in 2022 and charged after attempting a coup that reportedly involved plans to assassinate Lula . Then in September 2025, when Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence for leading the coup attempt, the pair pivoted to his son, according to the report. Both men advocated for punitive measures to weaken Lula, including the designation of Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and the imposition of sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who led investigations into Jair Bolsonaro, Reuters reported. Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro promised to seek amnesty for his father and the rioters who supported him, as well as impeachments for the Supreme Court justices who jailed them, according to the New York Times . But Lula stood up to Trump, refusing to drop coup charges against the elder Bolsonaro. While this act of resistance garnered Lula some support, it was not strong enough to win his initial contest against Bolsonaro earlier this month. The Brazilian incumbent won only 45 percent of the vote to Bolsonaro's 47 percent, triggering a runoff as neither met the nation's 50 percent requirement for victory. Poggio believes this initial defeat worked in the favor of the Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT)or Workers Party, and Lula, who won on Sunday by 4 million votes. "Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead encouraged some complacency among supporters who believed the election was largely won," Poggio said. "Lula’s defeat instead generated urgency: the PT reactivated its grassroots organization, while unions, social movements, artists, intellectuals and civil-society figures turned the runoff into a broader mobilization against the return of bolsonarismo." That grassroots organization moved fast to deliver what Poggio described as "a concrete economic message" from Lula. Brazilians were promised a "pacote de bondades” or “goodies package” that included a 15 percent increase in Bolsa Família, a financial aid program for Brazil's lower income citizens, as well as fuel-tax reductions, debt relief and education and transportation initiatives, Poggio said. All the while, Bolsonaro struggled to present an equally strong counterpoint, said Poggio. "He promised to maintain or expand Bolsa Família and other popular programs associated with Lula, while retreating from some unpopular positions," said Poggio. "This allowed Lula to argue that voters could preserve social protections without accepting the political and institutional risks associated with the Bolsonaro family’s return." Brazilian voters were not alone last week in rejecting the risks involved with a Trump ally's leadership. In Serbia, President Aleksandar Vučić lost control of his government to a group of academics, professionals and public figures who call themselves the Student List and protested their government's increasingly authoritarian measures. And in April, Hungary's leader Viktor Orbán — an autocrat and staunch Trump supporter — was thrown from power in a popular vote. On Tuesday, Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu faces the possibility of joining Bolsonaro, Vučić and Orban's ranks as he bids for reelection amid wars in Gaza and Iran that Trump is also involved in. Left-leaning leaders across the world were celebrating Lula's victory Monday. Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum called it a win for democracy and the people of Brazil. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez replied to the news , "The global progressive resurgence has just begun." Poggio concurs the Brazilian vote will serve as a vital check. "Lula’s victory interrupts that rightward momentum and preserves Brazil as a counterweight to Washington," he said, "committed to multilateralism, regional autonomy and relations with the Global South."
